title: Who gains when disinflation lengthens European saving?
summary: Christian Noyer argued that price stability could change both the maturity of European saving and the firms able to obtain it. An unexpected price increase erodes the purchasing power of cash, fixed-rate deposits and bonds. More predictable inflation should make households more willing to tie up savings for longer. Separately, one currency and more liquid securities markets could channel those savings to a broader set of borrowers. For an investor, the distinction matters. Lower compensation for inflation uncertainty can reduce a borrower’s cost of capital while lowering the prospective yield earned by a new bond buyer. Wider access to credit can expand issuance even if the saving rate itself changes little.

The exposure to inflation differed sharply by instrument. Cash and sight deposits, with little or no remuneration, represented 39% of M3 in 1999. That is a share of a monetary aggregate, not the share of household wealth held as cash. Fixed-term deposits can reprice only on specified dates or with a lag. A bond coupon may embed the inflation expected at issue, leaving its holder exposed to subsequent surprises. Where tax is levied on nominal interest including compensation for the loss of purchasing power, the real return to a creditor can decline further. Noyer argued that less well-off savers often lacked the information needed to protect themselves. He also saw a possible reduction in total saving if households became less willing to save under inflation uncertainty, or if redistribution from private agents towards a public sector with a lower saving ratio reduced saving overall (section 1).

Uncertain prices also complicate the choice of projects. Interest receipts including an inflation premium, or simply the gap between the date a firm incurs an expense and the date it receives payment, can distort accounts. A borrower may benefit from erosion in the real value of its liabilities without any underlying improvement in the profitability of production. Noyer thought clearer price signals and lower inflation premia in real financing costs could favour productive investment. Observations on financial liabilities alone cannot show which borrowers turned new funding into productive assets or when income from those investments might accrue.

Noyer offered three different pieces of evidence for longer commitments. Life insurance absorbed 26% of the investment flows of euro-area non-financial agents on average in 1997–98, up from 18% at the beginning of the 1990s. Long-term financial liabilities of monetary financial institutions grew 7.2% in the twelve months to November 1999. And bond issuance rose during 1999. The first statistic is a share of new investment flows, the second a growth rate for liabilities of financial institutions, and the third an issuance observation. Noyer himself recognised that the removal of internal exchange-rate risk and deeper markets also spurred bond issuance. The figures support a possible shift towards longer maturities. They cannot isolate the effect of monetary policy on saving, as opposed to a change in the instruments used to hold it.

Retirement financing made this distributional issue more pressing. Public spending in 1999 represented 49% of GDP in the euro area, 39% in Japan and 34% in the US. Those figures cover all public spending, not pension spending. With treaty limits on public deficits and price stability limiting the inflationary erosion of liabilities, Noyer saw an important future role for private retirement savings. The speech does not quantify a pension funding gap, or establish that longer-duration saving by some groups can protect households unable to save in the first place.

Market integration was furthest advanced where payments infrastructure supported it. The TARGET large-value payment system and rapid acceptance of EONIA and EURIBOR helped short rates converge. Bond, repo and short-term securities markets still faced differences in property rights, payment arrangements, taxation, accounting and supervision. Sovereign yield differentials had narrowed considerably during 1998, and euro bond issuance by private non-financial firms in the first ten months of 1999 was three times that in the same period of 1998. Smaller and lower-rated companies were gaining access. More issuance increases choice and may reduce the liquidity compensation demanded by investors. The volume alone does not show that spreads on lower-rated borrowers covered the credit risk being assumed (section 2).

The same changes put intermediaries under pressure. The number of monetary financial institutions fell 5% in the year to November 1999, extending a pre-existing decline. Private databases put the value of mergers and acquisitions involving euro-area banks in 1999 about 35% above the 1998 level. These are different measures of restructuring. Neither quantifies savings passed on to households or demonstrates that consolidation made the surviving institutions safer. Noyer ended by identifying conditions that could undermine his case, including insufficient fiscal consolidation absorbing private funds, taxation, wages growing out of line with productivity, and financial instability. He described the Eurosystem as monitoring banking risks and asset prices relevant to stability while lacking direct prudential authority at the time.

questions.question: Did households save more, or move existing financial flows into insurance and longer maturities?
questions.detail: Compare flow-of-funds accounts, household saving rates and the maturity composition of financial assets within the same countries and years. Examine insurance taxation and pension reforms alongside inflation trends. An allocation shift can support duration demand even if the supply of fresh household saving rises little.

questions.question: How much did the all-in cost of capital fall for smaller or lower-rated borrowers?
questions.detail: Match new issues to incumbent firms and comparable bank loans by currency, maturity and risk. Separate credit spreads, issuance fees and liquidity premia. Evidence from prospectuses and subsequent uses of proceeds available at the time would clarify whether cheaper finance funded investment, refinancing or a balance-sheet transfer.

questions.question: Which savers actually gained purchasing power after taxes?
questions.detail: Use household portfolios by income and age, deposit repricing terms and national rules on nominal interest. Compare realised real after-tax returns on deposits and bonds as inflation fell. The result matters for the incidence of disinflation and for the durability of the retirement-saving demand Noyer anticipated.

questions.question: Did consolidation improve liquidity at the cost of concentrating intermediation risk?
questions.detail: Consult contemporaneous national supervisory statistics, market-maker participation and bank accounts alongside payment and settlement data. Compare lower transaction costs with the availability of liquidity outside benchmark issues. A deeper primary market does not by itself establish reliable exit liquidity for portfolios.
